FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 171) respecting the government guaranteed bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific. He said : The first purpose of this Bill is to authorize the Grand Trunk Pacific to pledge the bonds guaranteed by the government as security for the raising of money. The earliest legislation undoubtedly contemplated that the company should have the power to pledge the bonds as well as sell them. It would seem, however, that the machinery provided is inadequate and it is necessary to specifically give the com-Mr. NORTHRUP.
pany the power to pledge the bonds. If the market were deemed unfavoui'able to press the sale of the bonds, the company might raise money by pledging the bonds as collateral security. The second purpose of the Bill is due to certain judicial decisions given in England to the effect that when a bond is pledged in the way contemplated by this Bill, it is deemed to have been issued and the power of the company to sell it ceases. Consequently w'hen the bonds given as collateral security are restored to the possession of the company the company would not have the legal right to sell them. To remove all possible doubt, we propose to declare that the pledging of the bonds will not interfere with the right of the company to sell them at a later stage. The same difficulty will probably come up in connection with other companies and it may be necessary to pass general legislation upon. the subject. In the meantime, ns we are dealing with this particular case, we ask that the company be given the power to pledge the bonds as security in order to raise money and that this shall not interfere with their right to sell the same bonds when the company again obtain possession of them. The third purpose of the Bill is intended to facilitate the operations of the company in the construction of the railway. To avoid delays which, it has been found by experience, sometimes happen, and enable the company to make prompt payment for work done, it is proposed that we give them a letter of credit, practically as we do now in connection with our own departments, authorizing the company to expend a limited sum, not exceeding at any time the sum of one million dollars. That letter of credit is to be dealt with in the same way as a letter of credit under our ordinary financial operations. The expenditure must of necessity be used for the purpose authorized by the Transcontinental Railway Act. At regular intervals, say at the end of each month, the chief engineer must examine these expenditures and if they all fall under the Act and are such as he can certify to, he will certify accordingly. If it be found that, under this letter of credit, the company have used the proceeds thus obtained, or any part thereof, for any purposes not entirely within the meaning of the Act, then the sum so used must instantly be made good by a deposit in the bank to the credit of the same fund from which they were withdrawn. Before any letter of credit shall be issued, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which is the parent company, must enter into an agreement to make good any money which may be expended in the unauthorized way to which I have referred. These are the three purposes of the Bill.

I would like to ask the Finance Minister if he does not think this

is one of the Bills which should be introduced by way of resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At one time I was inclined to think as does my hon. friend, but I took advice on that point. It is not the money of the Consolidated Fund of Canada but money which belongs to the Grand Trunk Pacific, but inasmuch as it is raised on the credit of the government of Canada it is placed in a special account to the credit of the Minister of Finance and Receiver General and can only be drawn upon on certificates of the government engineer. The government therefore supervise the money very properly, but it is not a part of the consolidated fund. However, even if it were a part of the consolidated fund, this Bill does not create any new obligation in any way ; it simply gives directions as to the manner in which the fund already created shall be distributed. It does not create a new obligation or add to any former obligation of the government.
Does it not give power to raise money ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it does not give power to raise money in the sense in which the word is used by my hon. friend ; the power to raise money has already been given by the granting of power to issue the bonds. This is a power to take the bonds to the bank, and to say : We do not find it expedient owing to circumstances to sell these bonds at present but we will leave them here as collateral. That is a power which all railways have under the General Railway Act, but for the special reasons in this ease it is necessary to introduce this Bill. There is nothing unusual in the Bill, I have had it looked into and I do not think it is necessary to adopt the suggestion that has been made.
I understand the credit is based on money already in the funds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite so, and only on the money derived from these bonds. It is not a letter of credit on the consolidated fund at all.
It is not an advance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Before you leave the chair, I would like to bring to the attention of the House very briefly the circumstances attending the loss or destruction of the papers connected with the Stan-stead election of 1908. I thought the matter of sufficient importance to justify me in procuring a copy of the evidence which is too long to read to the House, but the facts in which I shall bring to the attention of membe'-s. In the first place it would appear that the present Clerk of the Crown in Chancery received a letter from the soli-Mr. MONK.
eitor of the petitioner on the 23rd of April, 1908, inquiring who was the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery at that date and asking that information for the purpose of serving a subpoena upon him in order that be might pioduce papers relative to the by-election in Stanstead in 1908, which was then under consideration upon the proceedings already taken in the court. It would appear that that letter was answered by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery on the 24th of April and that before answering the letter, the purport of which does not appear from the evidence, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery made search in his office and discovered that the papers referred to, that is the papers relating to the by-election of 1908, were missing and that in the box or place where he might have expected to fiud them he found instead the papers relating to the Stanstead general election of 1904. It does not appear that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery made any communication whetever of this very important fact to the solicitor	of	the petitioner,	and Igather from what	has been said	by	the
right hon. the Prime Minister that he was consulted upon the subject by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery immediately after the loss of the papers was discovered.
I would not have brought the matter up for the purpose of making the observation I am about to make, but I think it is pertinent to make	it	in this connection.	Itwould seem to	me	to be the duty	of	the
Clerk of the Crown in Chancery-and it would have been proper for the Prime Minister to have advised the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery of that duty-to acquaint at once the solicitor of the petitioner with the fact that public documents of this country, properly required for the purposes of a trial which would determine the right to a seat in this House, could not be found and were either destroyed or stolen or made away with in some manner. It is perfectly obvious to any bon. gentleman in this House who realizes the importance of this matter, that that should have been done. To prove the election properly under such conditions it would be necessary to have certain searches made and certain inquiries carried on in order that secondary evidence of that which would be properly proved by the best evidence, might be admitted by the judge presiding at the inquiry. If it had happened that the judge presiding at that inquiry had not granted an adjournment, very serious consequences might have followed the failure of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to adopt the course which I have suggested as a proper one for him to adopt. As a matter of fact, the counsel for the petitioner with whom I have conversed on this subject, states to me that he did not know until the witness actually went upon the stand and gave his evidence, that the papers would not be forthcoming ; and although he made

inquiries from Mr. Foley after his arrival at Sherbrooke, as to the production of the papers, he was unable to obtain any information upon that subject.
Now the facts seem to be these : in the first place, let me say at once that whatever suspicion, if there be any suspicion, may attach to the loss of these papers-and X am not suggesting any suspicion at the present moment-the late Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, Mr. Lamothe, is absolutely above any suspicion whatever, either as to his character or his ability. All who knew that gentleman realize that the proper discharge of his duties of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery was his chief consideration, and no one would for a moment suppose that he would be concerned in any way, either directly or indirectly in any act at all improper in connection with these papers or any others. His assistants and clerks I believe to be equally reliable and faithful. It appears that Mr. Lamothe fell ill in March, and that during the mouth of March he suffered more or less from the disorder which eventually carried him off. It appears further that the papers relating to the Stanstead by-election had been received on the 5th day of February by registered mail from the returning officer ; and also that a man by the name of L'Heureux came to the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery on the 8tli or 10th of February in order to ascertain if any papers in that office were ready to be taken away and burned. I should perhaps state in this connection that it is the practice, in the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery as in other departments of government, to give to this man, who has some contract or mandate for that purpose, the papers which are useless and which it is desired to get out of the way. He came on the Sth or 10th of February, but the evidence is not very plain, so far as I can understand it, whether he actually took away some papers at that time, but it is probable that he did so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Who is L'Heureux ?

L'Heureux is a carter or a man of that class, who is employed in the various departments of the government, and in this building I think, to come and take away the papers that are put aside as waste and useless. I understand that he takes them away and destroys them in a furnace. It appears that L'Heureux went to the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery about the 8th or 10th of February, and it would appear probable that he did take away some papers on that occasion. But it is to be remembered that the papers relating to the StarTstead election had been received in the office of the Clerk of the Crown in
Chancery only three days before. The papers are kept in the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, in pigeon holes, each one having a door which is fastened by a key, and I believe that one or two keys fit practically nearly all the locks on these pigeon holes.
Mr. Lamothe was last in his office on the 1st day of April, 1908, and he died on the 8th day of April. He was subpoenaed to attend the hearing of the preliminary objections apparently for the 6th day of April, 1908. I gather that by inference rather than by direct statement. It would appear that the hearing was adjourned in consequence of his illness to the 6th day of May. At all events he was subpoenaed on the 1st day of April, and that was the day on which he last attended in his office. Mr. Chadwick, a clerk in the office, declares in his testimony that lie saw the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery get the papers ready after receiving the subpoena on the 1st day of April. He is not sure as to the date, and he says further in his evidence that in the ordinary course Mr. Lamothe would have done this about two days after receiving the subpoena. He seems to be confident however that he saw him get the papers ready for the purpose of taking them to the hearing of the preliminary objections. If that is correct, and I think it is, Mr. Lamothe must have done that on the 1st day of April, the very day on which he received the subpoena, because he was not in his office after that date.
Mr. Foley was appointed Clerk of the Crown in Chancery on the 21st day of April. During the interim there was no person specially charged with the duties of the office, except in so far as Mr. Chadwick and the young lady stenographer who was employed in the office, might be considered as invested with any mandate to discharge such duties. Mr. Foley, the present Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, attended at the preliminary objections on the 6th day of May, when he made known for the first time the fact that the papers were missing. He says that after receiving his subpoena to attend the hearing he immediately proceeded to look for the paper's, and he then discovered the box bearing the label ' Stanstead by-election, 1908,' and he proceeded to get those papers ready to take with him in attending the court in obedience to the subpoena; and happening by accident to look into one of the envelopes, he discovered that these papers were really the papers for the general election of 1904, and not for the by-election of 1908. He discovered, however, in the box, along with the other documents, the stamp used for the purpose of the by-election of 1908, but he did not discover the stamp used for the election of 1904. The stamp of course does not accompany the copy of the deposition which I have, but an impression had been

forwarded. It is just a stamp containing the words ' Returning officer, Stanstead, 1908.' I will not weary the House with reading any portion of the evidence giving Mr. Foley's explanation of the presence of that stamp. I could not follow very clearly the explanation, and I am inclined to think that there has been some mistake on the part of the stenographer in taking down the evidence. That of course very often occurs. For example, on the top of page 4, he gives the following answer :
Did you make search yourself?-A. Yes, Sir, I made most diligent search myself and also my deputy Mr. Chadwick whom I called in at once. And we both made all possible search for the papers, but could find nothing else. Mr. Chadwick afterwards went to Mr. Lamothe's house and made search there without avail. The only evidence I could find of the 1908 election in the box, is the little stamp that I have here (witness produced a rubber stamp). I suppose that was on account of the box being placed on one end, this remained on the bottom.
It is the last sentence of the testimony which I have just read that I do not understand. It does not afford to me, at least, an adequate explanation of how it was that althougn all the other papers relating to the Stanstead election of 1908 disappeared, this rubber stamp was found in the box where these papers should also have been found. So much for the circumstances of the case.
Would it not have been thrown in outside of the envelope ?

I do not know whether or not the evidence gives us any information in regard to that. I made some inquiry and I understand that the stamp might come back in a bag with other papers or it might come with another parcel.
I do not feel that too much importance should be attached to the fact that the stamp was found in the box. But, it is a singular circumstance that every other paper which should have been found in the box had disappeared and that the stamp of 1908 was found there while the stamp of 1904 was not found there. The matter with which I jam chiefly concerned, in bringing this subject to the attention of the House, is this : the evidence disloses that a great many persons have access to the office, persons employed in the building who require to visit the different rooms for any purpose, all these possess keys to this room. For example, the engineers and other persons requiring to do any work in the different rooms of this building possess keys. The messengers of the House possess keys. I am not making reference to these persons with the slightest idea of casting suspicion upon them, but simply in connection with another circumstances which is of the gravest possible nature and it is that a great many keys are available for this room and any Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
person who can obtain access to this room, can, by using two or three keys, of the most ordinary description, find eventually a key which will open every one of these boxes and expose to that person public documents which may affect the seats of half a dozen members of this House. I have made inquiry on the subject heretofore and I understand that the officials of the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery have been asking for two years that they should be provided with steel file cases which would make these papers absolutely secure. These file cases would be provided with locks which would not be susceptible to being opened by such ordinary means as those I have indicated.
We do not know what may be the result of the loss or destruction in the present case. I do not desire to miake any comment upon the Stanstead election. I did not rise for the purpose of doing it, but let us assume an election in which there were not only genuine ballots but ballots fraudulent upon their face such as we discovered upon examination of the ballots of the West Huron and Brockville elections ; does not my hon. friend the Prime Minister, does not every member of this House, realize how absolutely essential it miay be to the interests of persons concerned in such frauds that the ballot papers in that particular case should be destroyed, and should not be forthcoming when they were called for upon the preliminary inquiry or any other inquiry 1 That emphasizes the absolute necessity of providing the clerk of the Crown in Chancery with proper steel cases secured by proper locks in order that public documents of this character which may be required in the courts of the country may be preserved and in order that parliament may be properly and regularly constituted. As I have said here I understand that has been the urgent wish of the officials in that department during the past two years and such a wish has been expressed on several occasions, to the proper authorities who have, up to the present time, absolutely disregarded it. Then, there is another suggestion that I would like to make to the government, that there should be some departmental inquiry or investigation, or an investigation by the House, if necessary-the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is attached to what department ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is attached to the House of Commons.
He is not attached to any particular department ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. When Mr. Lamothe was in office the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery was attached to the Department of the Privy Council and had been for some years, but it was suggested that he should be attached to the House of Commons to which he properly belongs

ana when we appointed a successor, Mr. Foley, we transferred him to the staff of the House of Commons.

I recollect that the right hon. Prime Minister announced that owing to the suggestion made by the Civil Service Commission that change had been made. It would seem very desirable that Mr. Speaker should make some investigation into this matter if it were not thought worthy of the attention of the Committee on Privileges and Elections. I would be inclined to think that an inquiry should be prosecuted at once. It is not for me to say how serious under the present circumstances may be the loss of these ballots. It is represented to me that the loss may be a very serious one in prosecuting the inquiry which it was proposed to carry on by the proceedings in the courts. I am not at the present time attaching blame to any of the officials. I have not the material upon which I could be justified in imputing blame to any official, and I should require circumstances of a very cogent nature before I would propose to cast that blame. But, there are two things which are absolutely certain. In the first place, Mr. Lamothe was not only a most conscientious officer, but he was a most careful and diligent officer in the discharge of his duties. One finds it difficult therefore to believe that on the 8th or 10th of February last, three days after he had received the papers relating to the by-election in Stanstead, he should have sent these papers away to be destroyed, making the mistake of believing that they were papers which had come to him in connection with the general election of 1904. I find it very difficult to bring myself to the conclusion that there was any such mistake as that and yet it is the only explanation which has been vouchsafed up to the present time. In the second place, I desire to call attention once more to the urgent, thorough necessity of providing the officials of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery with such steel cases, or other appliances of a like character, as will place suspicion of any wrong doing in connection with a matter of this kind absolutely be-voud question. At the present time we have this condition of affairs :	The
papers have been lost, a certain explanation has been given and that explanation depends upon the most remarkable negligence and inadvertence on the part of a very capable, reliable, diligent and conscientious officer. If we do not accept that explanation then we simply require to conjecture some other and it Is impossible to conjecture any other without at the same time casting suspicion which ought not to be cast without adequate and grave reasons. It surlev is undesirable that the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery should be accessible to so many persons and that it should not be provided with the means of
keeping these papers absolutely safe and secure Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I thought it nothing more than my duty to bring the matter to the attention of the government in the earnest hope that immediate steps will be taken so that an occurrence of this kind cannot possibly come again to the attention of the House.

My hon. friend has paid to the late Mr. Lamothe a tribute of which he was altogether worthy ; no more faithful officer ever lived. I may say also that to Mr. Chadwick, the other clerk in the office, the most unqualified commendation can be given.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chadwick is also a most honourable and painstaking officer. Mr. Foley, the present Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, is also a very excellent officer but of course he had nothing to do with this. The office of the council of the Crown in Chancery is in this building and Mr. Foley before his appointment was working in the Privy Council office in the eastern block. It is difficult to account for such an accident, but having given it consideration since it was brought to my attention I must say the conclusion I have arrived at is that the papers disappeared before the death of Mr. Lamothe. I do not care to enter into this further than to say that I believe it was the result of an accident and nothing else. I think everybody admits that. My hon. friend has stated that Mr. Lamothe and Mr. Chadwick of late years have repeatedly made applications for these steel cases. These applications would necessarily come to me first and if Mr. Lamothe did make such an application I must say that I do not remember it. If a requisition of that kind should come to me, after having discussed it with the officers I would send it immediately to the Department of Public Works. But I have no recollection of having received such an application although it is quite possible it may have been made. As to the suggestion that the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is accessible to several people, I think that applies to every office in the departments, for the charwomen must go there every morning and other people must of necessity have access.

Of course that is absolutely necessary and I was not objecting to it. I merely mentioned it to show the necessity for providing these steel file cases so that those who go into the office could not get at the papers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery properly belongs to this House and there is no reason at all why it should be attached to

any department of the government. When the commission reported that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery should be on the staff of the Honse of Commons it seemed to be perfectly reasonable, and when we appointed a successor to Mr. Lamothe we put him at once on the staff of this House and he is now under the jurisdiction of Mir. Speaker and not under the President of the Privy Council as wias formerly the case. The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is the custodian of the archives connected with elections to this House and he therefore holds a very important position. I welcome the suggestion that we should have an investigation so that attention may be given to the advisability of taking extra precautions for the keeping of these records. If it be the wish of my hon. friends opposite I should be quite willing to consent to the appointment of a special committee to investigate the whole question. I may say that the matter was brought to my attention for the first time shortly after Mr. Foley assumed office. He came to my room in the House of Commons, on what date I do not remember further than it was Friday afternoon and he had been summoned to appear at the trial on the following Tuesday. I advised Mr. Foley to at once report to the Speaker of {he House and to get from the Printing Bureau a list of the electors so that If the solicitor for the petitioners wanted secondary evidence, that might facilitate the proceedings. I repeat that we are only too happy to have any further investigation as to the cause of the accident, if the cause can be found, and with a view of guarding against as far as possible any such accident taking place in future.
This matter has been known for some time; is it true that up to the present no special investigation has been made?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No special investigation has been made and I do not see what special investigation could be made. Nobody blames Mr. Lamothe and everybody must come to the conclusion that it was merely an accident. If there was any reason to suppose that there had been dishonest design in the destruction of these ballots the case would be different, but I cannot see for what purpose anybody would destroy these ballots.
The purpose is very evident.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not evident at all. As I understand it the controversy in the courts is simply as to a matter of form and the Clerk of the Crown In Chancery was summoned to give the usual formal evidence as to the holding of the election. These papers having been destroyed it is not difficult at all to make secondary evidence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. FOSTER, if the process is to eventuate in anything, the case would come to trial and then the ballots would be important, and the ballots have gone.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I have been informed, the preliminary objection has been taken in the trial that the returning officer did not initial or certify the lists which were delivered to the deputy returning officers, and if that be the point it can be determined by secondary evidence. As a fact I understand the returning officer admits he did not sign these papers.

The Prime Minister is quite right that secondary evidence could be produced and it would be foolish for any one to suppose that the petition would be absolutely defeated by destroying the ballots. But the importance of the ballots does not cease there, because if certain fraudulent acts have been committed at certain polls the production of the ballots would be an important feature.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Undoubtedly.
I am informed by the counsel for the petitioner that he regards the ballots as very important evidence for his client.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is the first intimation I have of that.

The really important point is that it is possible for ballots to be destroyed in any way. thus rendering the restitution of his rights to an aggrieved candidate practically impossible. Surely it is important that such an occurrence should be inquired into. The gravity of the whole thing, I think, is in that. Granted that Mr. Lamothe was not to blame-and in that opinion I agree heartily with the Prime Minister and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition-the ballots have disappeared. It is just as fair to suppose that Mr. Lamothe did not by accident destroy the ballots or allow them to be destroyed, as it is to suppose that he may have committed an error unwittingly and thereby the ballots have gone. It is just as easy, and I* think much more natural, to suppose that a third party has been able to intervene, and for some purpose or other to do away with the ballots. I would rather suppose that than that Mr. Lamothe, a very careful officer, who has been in that office for a long while, could have allowed the ballots to have been taken away in mistake for those of 1904 ; and it is to me a little startling that the Prime Minister seems to have thought that it was quite well enough to let the matter slip along and to make no investigation of it at all, but only now is willing to take the suggestion that has been miade.
It seems to me that such a thing ought immediately to have been put in the hands of the Dominion police. They work by
8S49

clues, and might have been able to discover whether or not some third party had intervened and had made away with the ballots. That is a supposition that is quite plain to be taken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My opinion and my information is that there was nobody to blame, but that it was an accident ; but I concur in the suggestion of my hon. friend that the matter should be investigated by a special committee of this House with the view of ascertaining the cause and what precautions may be taken to prevent similar accidents in the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the right hon. leader of the House has explained, it is only recently that the officer has been transferred to the jurisdiction of the House of Commons. I am aware that since that transfer has been made, Mr. Speaker has communicated with Mr. Foley, now the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, and has requested him to make suggestions as to what improvements he would wish to have made for the better care of the documents, in the way of improved accommodation or otherwise. No doubt, if there has been any laxity, the necessary arrangements will be speedily made for the better care of the documents in the future. Mr. Speaker has already taken action for that purpose.

The peculiarly regrettable feature of the matter seems to be this. We have had twice in the history of Canada the destruction of ballots and papers that were supposed to be necessary and valuable for determining the result of a contest in the courts over elections, once in Toronto, and once here ; and is it not striange that the papers in both cases disappeared apparently at the very time they were most needed, and that the history of the loss appears to have been exactly the same in both cases-they were destroyed by accident ? In the West Elgin case the ballots were burned, as it was said to be the custom to burn the biallot papers after they were several years old ; and those which had come in recently got mixed with the old ones. Does it look natural or reasonable, that any business man charged with the responsibility of keeping the papers relating to an election of three or four years ago would allow them to get mixed up with the papers relating to an election of only a month ago ? It does not seem to me to be natural or probable or .reasonable. Therefore, while not desiring to say too much on this matter, I cannot refrain from the suspicion that there is fault somewhere, and that the act was the result of design rather than of accident. In both cases the papers were destroyed just when an election contest was going on in the courts, and when the destruction of the papers would serve the interests of the same
political party, once in the province and once in the Dominion. Another strange coincidence is that an important member of the cabinet was the confidential adviser of the party in Ontario at the time that this happened there, and when the fact came out the same explanation was given that is given to-day in this instance. This shows either that great minds run in the same channel or that it was really and purely a coincidence. Another feature that seems to be interesting is the fact that when the matter was brought to the attention of the government, they made no effort to ascertain the cause of it. The destruction of these papers might result in keeping a member improperly sitting in this House for the remainder of the term, or they might put him out of the House by disclosing irregularities or devices that in law would be very serious punishable offences. But the destruction of the papers destroyed all that. The very fact that these weighty consequences were involved, and that it is very desirable that all public officers should be above suspicion with regard to the faithful and careful discharge of their duties, should have led to a most searching inquiry at the earliest possible moment so as to satisfy all that it was purely and simply an accident and nothing else. If that had been done, the incident would have ended there ; but the indifference of the government with regard to it in itself creates the suspicion that they did not think it worth while to have an inquiry made until some one brought it to the attention of the House, and then they say if the House desires they will have an inquiry. If such a thing had happened with the other party, either in this House or in Ontario. I venture to think that not a moment's delay would have occurred before a most searching inquiry would have taken place to ascertain what was the real history of the destruction of these important papers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To-morrow I will move that this matter be referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections, or, if hon. gentlemen prefer, to a select committee.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Agriculture to certain reports in the newspapers. It is stated in the ' Star ' of Monday, the 18th May, that at a meeting held at Knowl-ton on Saturday, the 16th. the Hon. Sydney Fisher, Minister of Agriculture, declared that ' provincial politics must go hand in hand with federal politics, for both are destined to work for the good of the country.' In the ' Herald ' of May 18 it is stated :

Hon. Mr. Fisher congratulated Mr. Vilas on his record at Quebec, and on the evident approval of the electors of Brorne. There was, he said, an intimate connection between the politics of the province and the politics *of the Dominion, because each was destined to conduct the country in the same paths of progress and prosperity.
The ' Free Press ' of May 15, giving a report of the meeting at the Russell House, reports the speech of the Hon. Mr. Graham thus :
He (Hon. A. G. Mackay) stood for the same Liberalism as did the federal party, and the Dominion leaders were behind him.
The 'Evening Journal' of the 15th May reports the same lion, gentleman thus :
I want to say that as a member of the federal government I believe in and support Mr. Mackay as the leader in Ontario.
I would ask the hon. gentlemen if they are reported correctly. Also, I would appreciate the courtesy if the right hon. leader of this House would say whether he approves of provincial issues being identified with federal politics ?

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: All 1 have to say is that I am a supporter of the Hon. A. G. Mackay in the province of Ontario and am proud of it. I do not propose to go into a discussion of political issue. Mr. Mackay is well able to do that himself. If he were holding a meeting to-morrow, and if I could get away, I would be on the platform behind him or beside him.

Before you leave the chair. Mr. Speaker, I would like to be permitted to make a few remarks regarding the abandonment by this government, to a great extent, of the military demonstration at the Quebec tercentenary. The present attitude of the government is an abandonment of the intended mobilization of the militia of Canada at that celebration. The matter is one, in my opinion, of very great, if not of immediate, public importance. The people of Canada have been led to believe by the government that at least fifty per cent of the Canadian militia, besides the permanent force, would be mobilized at Quebec on the occasion of the tercentenary celebration. When the Minister of Militia was passing some of his estimates, as far back as the 27th March last, the question came up and he then said, as far as I was then able to understand, that the government had made certain arrangements with regard to this matter. On that occasion hon. gentlemen on this side who spoke supported the proposition, and the House was unanimous in its approval [DOT]of the course then outlined by the hon. min-Mr ROBITAILLE.
ister to abandon the rural camps in the summer and have only one camp or mobilization of our militia on the Plains of Abraham or thereabouts at Quebec. On that occasion the government made a contract with this House and the people and the militia of this country that that proposal would be carried out. But we are now told something entirely different. We are told, if we are told anything definite, that it is proposed to abandon the position then taken for the reason that the transportation companies are unable or unwilling to convey the militia at a time when they hiave to convey such a large concourse of people as will necessarily go to Quebec. As early as 27th March last, the Minister of Militia, who ought to have been aware of the attitude of the transportation companies, said, as appears on page 5748 of 'Hansard':
The department appreciate the importance of this matter of transportation, and the very first thing we did was to address letters to all the transportation companies to ascertain what kind of accommodation they will be able to give us. The answers are coming in now.
Hear, hear.

That was as far back as the 27th March last, and it was not until the 13th May that this House was startled by the announcement of the Minister of Militia of the practical abandonment of this proposition. The government appointed a commission, and the members of that commission were appointed by the right hon. gentleman himself previous to the announcement of the Minister of Militia, and into the hands of that commission was committed the programme for the celebration at Quebec. It seemed to me that that was a matter which the government should not have delegated in that way. It seems to me that the duties were such as they should have performed themselves, and that they were in a better position to deal with these matters and the transportation companies than would be the commission. Be that as it may, the government appointed this commission, composed of very able men, and this commission mapped out a programme, which they published throughout Canada and the neighbouring republic and in fact the whole world. That programme consisted of four features. One was the mobilization of our military, which was practically Canada's only contribution to the event. Then there was to be a display of the British fleet, and I believe France and the United States were also asked to send warships to participate in that naval display, and then there was to be a grand pageant during eight or nine days depicting various scenes in the early history of this country, and in the end there was to be a display of fireworks and an illumination. The commission, on the faith of the government's attitude, and no doubt carrying out their instructions,

proceeded upon the basis that there was to be a mobilization of the army of Canada. That was something to be desired and which had not heretofore taken place in our history. The people were to be treated to a display of Canada's national army, mobilized to the extent of some 20,000 or 25,000 men. It was largely on that basis that the attraction of the celebration was based. That was to be the great attraction, as far as we are concerned in Canada. The British people were to contribute their quota towards the entertainment, and there is no reason to suppose that they will not carry out their engagement. The commission, haying made these tentative arrangements, proceeded to Quebec. I am informed that they went there in company with the officials of the Militia Council. At all events these officials went to Quebec and viewed the property where it was proposed to locate the camp, and in a general way mapped out arrangements for the accommodation of these men and for the carrying out of the military features. Let me say in passing that there can be no excuse for withdrawing the military mobilization scheme because of the lack of accommodation at Quebec, because the soldiers would in no way trespass upon the accommodation of civilians.
They would be provided with accommodation by the Department of Militia, entirely independent of the civilian quarters of the city so that they would not in any way interfere with the citizens. The commission proceeded upon that basis, so I am informed, and had interviews with the transportation companies who, while not anxious to undertake this matter, were ready to transport these troops and carry out the arrangement as intended, but in view of the expected congestion of traffic on the occasion, they asked to be allowed to take the troops down two days earlier and remove them from Quebec two days earlier than was otherwise intended. Even if the transportation companies were allowed to have their way, surely that was ground on which they could have been meet. If the abandonment of this whole matter hinged upon the presence of the troops there two days earlier than the people would arrive and their withdrawal two days earlier than the people would leave, surely that is a flimsy reason for the abandonment. Whether the transportation companies were right or wrong, if this arrangement could have been made to bring the troops there as I said two days earlier, it was surely worth while meeting them in that matter. The people were informed that these troops would be present, various contributions poured into the fund for this purpose, the province of Ontario contributed, I think, $100,000 and the province of Quebec $100,000, and there were other contributions from private persons, some in England and some in Canada. It seems to me that one feature of the programme on which these contributions were based was this military display. Why has it been abandoned? What sufficient reason is there for the abandonment? The military of this country were given to understand that they could have this opportunity of meeting in a joint camp. The citizen soldiery of the province of Ontario, and especially of Toronto, have looked forward to this, many of them have made their arrangements for the summer accordingly, the regiments have filled up to complete strength, and this is due in no small measure to the opportunity they expected would be afforded them in participating in this manoeuvre and going to Quebec. Is the government going to break faith with the people and with the military of this country? Surely some way can be found by w'hicb the original arrangement can be carried out. It seems altogether a flimsy excuse to say that the transportation companies must have their way in this matter and not carry these troops. The Minister of Militia would naturally be expected to know before he announced his scheme to the country whether or not the military could be entrained and properly handled. He said in this House on a subsequent occasion that the Militia Department could mobilize and handle twice that number of troops in 48 hours at a central point like Quebec where a number of railways centre. The commission have made their arrangements, the public have made their arrangements and now we are practically told that with the exception of the permanent force there is to be no military demonstration. That I think is not an unfair meaning to take from the remarks of the Minister of Militia who has said in the House :
A considerable portion of the permanent force will be sent to Quebec. What other portions will be sent I cannot say, but as soon as it is decided I shall be prepared to make an announcement to the House.
The impression has got abroad in this country that there is an abandonment of the whole military feature, except perhaps that it will be taken part in by the permanent force. If there is to be a renewal of this arrangement let it be announced at once. The time is approaching when the celebration is to be held. 25,000 men cannot get away on an hour's notice, and it seems to me the government have not kept faith with the militia or with the people of Canada or with this House. The railways, of course, expect a large concourse of people and the number who will attend is largely due, I believe, to the expected appearance of the military. When it is found thiat the military are not to appear it seems to me that Canada is practically abandoning all the portion that she was to contribute to that display. It is my opinion that the attendance will fall off in proportion. None of us want to see this cele-

bration a fizzle, we all want to see a large number of people there, but certainly if the plans at present contemplated by the government are pursued, there will be a great reduction in the number of people who will go there. If the government do not intend to abandon it they should, at the earliest possible moment, make an announcement to the country of what they intend to do so that people would know what part the military are to play in this celebration.

I wish to reassure my hon. friend at the outset that there has been no abandonment of anything. There has been a change of plans, although at the time this matter was first mentioned in the House, on the voting of certain supplies to the militia, to which my hon. friend has referred, I was very careful to say :
The plans have not yet been completed, in fact, they have scarcely been begun. It is the present idea that it would be desirable that a portion of the vote for the annual drill should be used in the transportation and mobilization of a considerable number of the militia at Quebec where they will be under canvass under the usual conditions of camp, and the duties ordinarily performed in camps of instruction will be discharged there, and of course the troops will take part in the review to be held at Quebec in connection with the celebration. I do not know how many days that will take, but whatever the cost will be it will be charged up against the vote for the annual drill and the officers of my department think that this will be a very valuable experience.
And so on. There was nothing definite and ' abandon ' is altogether too strong a term.
I thought it was announced afterwards that it was expected that 40,000 or 50,000 would be taken, or 50 per cent of the militia.

I said that 50 per cent of the active militia, the rural militia, would be taken, which would be about 20,000. The fact is that there will be a mobilization of a certain number of the militia of Canada at Quebec on this occasion, nobody has thought of abandoning that idea. I stated in the House the other day that it had been found impossible, on account of the difficulties connected with transportation, to mobilize such a large number as was at first thought of, some thirty odd thousand, and I stated that. would have interfered with one of the chief objects we have in view, namely, the bringing together at Quebec of a very large number of people from all over this continent, who will have to be brought there by the railways. After going into the thing carefully, the Quarter-Master General, who has charge of matters of transportaion, found that it would be very difficult indeed to carry out this mobilization.
Mr. MACDONELL
It would be full of risk, because accidents might arise in transporting guns, horses and all the paraphernalia attending a large camp, which would seriously interfere with the transportation facilities by which the people who expect to go to Quebec could alone be carried there. The other day I stated in the House fully the reasons why we had reluctantly given up the idea of a large camp which would practically include nearly the whole of the militia of Canada, but I said at the same time that there would be a force mobilized at Quebec. I do not suppose, Mr. Speaker, that there is any special advantage in making a military demonstration of great power and force at Quebec on that occasion. It does not seem to me that it is at all necessary. What I think we want is a fair representation of the militia of Canada, and that we expect to have, that, I think, is all that is necessary. I could go on and enlarge upon the subject, but I think I have said enough to satisfy any reasonable man. I am perfectly certain that I will be able to satisfy the militia of this country that we are doing what is in the interest of the militia itself. My hon. friend has stated that the militia regiments are all full now, beyond their normal strength even. Well, has it come to this, Mr. Speaker, that in order to have the regiments of the militia of Canada up to tilt full strength, it is necessary to provide some picnic such as they would expect to have on this visit to Quebec ? I have a higher opinion of the militia of Canada than that. I think they will be in full strength, and will attend to their duties at the camps this year just as well as they have ever done. I may say to my hon. friend that I have had many communications from different parts of Canada expressing pleasure at the fact that we have given up the idea of mobilizing the whole militia of the country at Quebec,
I would like the hon. minister to announce to the House what his programme is, and let the people know what the military features are going to be.

Precisely, and that is what I propose to do as soon as it is convenient. I said the other day when this question was brought up :
It is not correct to say that the troops are not going to the tercentenary. It is a fact, however, that the annual camps of instruction will be held as usual throughout the Dominion this year, instead of being held at one common point at or near the city of Quebec, as was proposed. The annual drill of the city regiments will also take place as usual this year. The reason of the change in the programme, which programme I announced briefly to the House three or four weeks.ago, is chiefly due to the difficulty of transportation. It will be understood, I am sure, that one of the principal things to keep in mind

in connection with this tercentenary celebration is to bring .together the largest number possible of people to Quebec to witness the ceremonies. Some time ago the chairman of the commission called my attention to the fact that the transportation lines, the railways and steamboats, must be left free as far as possible to bring the people to Quebec and take them home agajiq and he thought it proper to ask the Militia Department to agree not to move any troops on a certain ntimber of days before the celebration began and a certain number of days afterwards. It will be readily understood that such an arrangement would hamper the railway transportation lines very much. An earnest effort was made to see whether the difficulty could be overcome, but it was found it could only be partially overcome. It was therefore thought better that the camps should be held at the usual places of holding camps. As to the statement that has been made that the headquarters of the militia were unable to cope with the mobilization of 25,000 or 30,000 troops at a central point like Quebec, the story is absolutely without foundation, and is entirely absurd.
Then I went on to say that as soon as it was determined what number of troops would go to Quebec, I would make an announcement. I said that the Militia Department would be prepared to co-operate with the Battlefields Commission In every way in its power ; so it will be, and I hope before many days to be able to make an announcement to the House on that subject.

On the 27th of March I had the honour to ask the minister a question when this matter first came up. as will be seen on page 5711. I quite coincide with the opinion of the hou. member for Toronto (Mr. Mac-donell) that the minister has considerably changed front since that matter was first brought to his attention in the House. I asked the minister if the statement was correct which I had seen, that 60 per cent of the militia regiments would be taken to Quebec.
Is the percentage stated correct, 60 per cent?

About 50 per cent.
Here was an answer in distinct terms as to the number that were likely to go. Now the department seems to have retired from the position they took up at that time. At that time the matter appeared to be under the charge of the Militia Department entirely, and we were given to understand that it would be handled by the headquarters staff altogether. Now, If we are correctly informed, there has been a change, and the matter is to be handed over to the Quebec Battlefields Commission, because we see it stated in the papers that the Quebec Battlefields Commission are to select what regiments shall go to Quebec and what regiments shall not go.
I would ask my hon. friend to observe what I have said, not what the papers have said. I am not responsible for what the newspapers have said.
I hear what the minister says now, and I am not sure that he has always stated the same.
I read what I stated.

I have the very best information that that is not what took place the other day when a certain number of colonels and commanders of regiments appeared before the minister. What went out to the public at that time was practically what the member for South Toronto has said, that the Militia Department had entirely retired from the position they had taken of making a big military demonstration at Quebec, and that is the impression that prevails in all sections of the country.
. Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. Entirely erroneous.

I was told by more than one military man that the terms decided upon were such that it would be impossible for them to go, and the surrender of their pay and the difficulties that have been placed in their way would make it a financial impossibility for the regiments to go under the conditions named. Now if that is the case, it appears evident that Canada is to take a very little part in this great demonstration. If this demonstration means anything, it means a celebration of a military character, it is a military demonstration. We have fleets coming from Great Britain. No doubt if they hear on the other side that our militia are not going to take any part, that we have no fleet except the ice-breaker ' Montcalm.' and a few other disabled vessels, they will conclude, that we are practically out of it. Now we are told that even this military demonstration of which we expected so much, is going to be curtailed to such an extent that perhaps 3,000, or 4.000, or 5,000 may assemble. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this is a great and keen disappointment, not only to the militia, but to the citizens of Canada who look upon this as a great national occasion, an occasion when the patriotism of the people should be stirred, and when, if they were unable on account of financial or other reasons to go to Quebec themselves, they would take a keen interest in watching what was going on there, recognizing that we were celebrating the third centen-nary of an event which is very notable in Canadian history. I say it is to be deplored that the Militia Department are going back on what was expected of them. Whether it is going to be handled by the Battlefields Commission or the Militia Department, I think that the 50 per cent named in the

first place is not too great. The agreement was practically unanimous, as my hon. friend from South Toronto has said, no opposition developed on this side of the House.
Personally, I supported it very strongly as did several other gentlemen and I sincerely regret, Mr. Speaker, that the minister has apparently become comparatively lukewarm with regard to what was to be a great feature of the occasion. H<j told me, in reply to a question at the time, that the question of transportation was already engaging the attention of the department and that answers were coming in at that very time. Transportation could be easily managed if taken hold of in time. The river is open, there are plenty of first-class boats to be obtained and practically the whole western peninsula of Ontario could be served by the water route much more expeditiously and cheaply than in any other way. I believe that information has already been received by some gentlemen who have made inquiry that large boats can be obtained at a comparatively small cost for the transportation of the men and then they will feed them at the same price that the railway companies will charge for transportation alone. That is a statement that I received the other day from a gentleman who is thoroughly conversant with the question. If the railway and transportation companies of this country cannot take charge of the transportation of all these men, the United States alongside, I believe have intimated that they will allow the troops to pass through their territory if the request is made. I do not know that that is official, but at any rate I have it on good authority that some of the American railway companies have stated that they will see to it, if necessary, that troops are transported more cheaply in first-class cars than can be done by the Militia Department in box cars on this side. In that case why could we not send one, two, three, four or five regiments through the United States ? It might appear humiliating that we had to avail ourselves of American transportation for such an event but still it would be worth while making the attempt. I trust that such oilers will be received by the minister in the spirit in which they are conceived. The people are desirous of having a splendid demonstration on that occasion and they want to show what the Canadian militia system is. There has never been an opportunity in modem times when the minister and the department had such a chance of distinguishing themselves as they have on this occasion. To hand it over to the Battlefields Commission and to load them up with something that they do not want would be to make an unnecessarily large addition to their other duties and with the very expensive staff that we have in the Militia Department at Ottawa Mr. COCKSHUTT.
we should be able to place in the city of Quebec, 20,000 or 25,000 troops without seriously interfering with the ordinary traffic of the country. I think it can be done. I think that I am voicing the desire of the people and of the militia and when a great national occasion of this kind occurs and when we have an opportunity to show what the Canadian militia is and what our transportation facilities are it would be a pity if we should not take advantage of the occasion. There will be some large ships from across the water at Quebec. I understand the French Republic is going to be represented officially, the British government will be represented, the Prince of Wales will be there, an impression will be made that will be carried all over the world and if we fail to do what is expected of us I think we will do an injury to the country and an injury to the militia system of which we all to-day have every reason to be proud. I trust that the minister will give this his earnest and most serious consideration and that within a very few days he will come down with a statement that will be more satisfactory to the House and the country in regard to this tercentenary celebration that we are holding In the city of Quebec in the latter part of July.

If my hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) will permit me, I desire to say that I think a mistake was made by the department in issuing orders to" the regimental commanders with reference to the tercentenary until the arrangements were absolutely conclusive as to the transport of the troops. I do not think my hon. friend quite realizes the amount of disappointment that has ensued among the rural corps at any rate in consequence of the change of plan affecting them in going to the tercentenary. The orders issued to the commanding officers were to have fifty per cent of their respective commands in readiness.
No, there were no orders issued at all.
These were from the district officers.
Inquiries were sent to see what could be done. No general orders were issued whatever.
I think the minister is making a mistake in regard to that.
No, I looked it up to-(Iay because I knew this was coming up.

I will have to produce the orders to convince the minister. But, certain papers were issued-we will not call them orders for the present-advising the commanding officers to have fifty per cent of their respective commands in readiness
8S61

to go to Quebec. Another order, or another paper, came out a day or two afterwards requesting the commanding officers to say to their respective commands that they hoped they would understand that they might have to be transported in box cars. Surely, if it were not the intention to take them to Quebec it would not be necessary for the commanding officers of regiments to advise their officers and men that this was proposed to be done.

That is entirely a mistake. Certain inquiries were made, and, owing to the difficulty at the very outset as to this question of transportation, it was thought wise to ask the commanding officers of the regiments, through the regular channel, whether, in the event of there being a difficulty about transportation, they would be willing to go in box cars. They were to have their option. If they did not choose to go that way they need not go. It was thought wise to point out at the outset the difficulties that there would be and that there would be a possibility of the accommodation not being such as we would like to give them. There were no orders ; it was simply an inquiry.

Unfortunately I have not the papers here. I accept the statement of the minister, as I am bound to do, and I am perfectly certain he would not say that unless he was sure he was correct. At a later stage, I will have an opportunity of showing him the particular papers that I refer to. But, that is beside the question. What I wish to state, in so far as the rural regiments are concerned, is that I know, as a matter of fact, a number of regiments in our district have been drilling for the last three weeks in anticipation of going to Quebec. There is no doubt about that; I have seen them myself. It is a matter of keen disappointment to these men in the rural districts that they are not to take part in the celebration. I believe that it would be a good idea in the educative sense. There are thousands of young men in the rural districts who will never have an opportunity of seeing Quebec and I am sure the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) would like the members of the militia force to visit Quebec upon that occasion. We all take the greatest possible interest in the old city with its historical and other associations. It is a disappointment to these men in the rural districts because they will never have another opportunity such as this to visit the old city associated as it is with the history of the country. There is another thing that I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Militia to and it is that in a- pecuniary sense a good many of the officers are suffering. I happen to know that uniforms have been ordered by officers expecting to go, and which will have to be accepted
notwithstanding the fact that these officers may not go to Quebec. There are many things that the minister should consider. If there is any possibility of a change with regard to the rural regiments taking part in the celebration I trust the Minister of Militia will seriously consider the carrying out of the plan as at first proposed.

I understand the Minister of Militia has stated that that the Battlefields Commission are to make a selection from the different city corps.
ISir FREDERICK BORDEN. I never said that
Mr. PORTER, I have been informed that it was the intention to hand over the selection of the different corps to the Battlefields Commission.
There has been no arrangement of the kind.

There is a feeling of great disappointment among the volunteers in the district which I represent that they are not to be permitted to join in the celebration. They are chagrined that they are not to be allowed to exhibit their proficiency and their military spirit which they have so well demonstrated on many occasions in the defence of their country. They feel their services to the country in the past have been such as to entitle them to be selected for duty at Quebec, if any city corps is to be selected. I speak more particularly in reference to the 15th Argyle Light Infantry.
It is a good regiment.

R, LALOR (Haldimand). The officers and men of the 37th Battalion of Haldimand have been expecting to go to the historic city of Quebec, and they will be greatly disappointed if the Militia Department decides that they are not to go. speechtext: In this estimate we ask provision for 700 men; 500 in Alberta and Saskatchewan, 100 in what is now the Northwest Territories, and, 100 in the Yukon. We are gradually reducing the force in the Yukon. I think we have only eighty-two men there now and henceforward we intend to make no distinction between those in the Yukon and the rest of the force except as to pay.
What men have you in Manitoba?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have no men in Manitoba except one or two who form a cordon on the boundary to protect the revenue.
How are the one hundred men distributed in the Northwest Territories ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
At Churchill there are eight or ten men, at Fullerton an island on the west shore of the Hudson bay, five men; at Fort Maepherson, at the mouth of the Mackenzie river, four or five men; at Herschel island, four or five men. There are men on the Peace river, at Stone lake and other places. I have here a map, showing the distribution of the force, which I will lay on the table. We have a patrol Mr. L4LOR.
from Winnipeg to Fort Churchill to assert our authority on the Hudson bay. Some years ago we commenced to assert our authority both on the Hudson bay and on the Arctic ocean at Herschel island, because we found that American whalers were going there without authority. Since the police have taken possession and asserted our authority, the American whalers have taken licenses from us and have paid customs duties, and our authox-ity is no longer disputed. At first these American whalers were inclined to demur, and I think they made some complaint at Washington; but of late years we have had no trouble. We have a patrol from Winnipeg to Fort Churchill and a patrol from Dawson to Herschel island, so that at present our jurisdiction is fully established.

The mounted police who have asserted the sovereignty of Canada on those exposed portions of Hudson bay, are the permanent emblems of authority; they are always there, and they have force as well as appearance. The Prime Minister has said that although at first the American whalers were a little obstreperous and did not wish to take out licenses and pay customs duties, yet now everything is peaceably acknowledged and our sovereignty in those portions of the northwest and northeast is permanently established. If that be so, what is the use of sending Captain Bernier on an expedition this year and next year at an expense of hundreds of thousands of dollars? I am not finding fault with this in any party sense or wish to make party capital. I am simply asking the Prime Minister seriously to consider whether or not this should be allowed to go on under the plea of pi-otecting the sovereignty of Canada where absolutely nobody questions it. The United States has not raised a cavil with reference to our authority. These American whalers take out their licenses and pay their customs dues to the Mounted Police, who are the customs officers. Is not that sufficient? If it costs a good deal, the country is quite willing to pay the necessary cost. Why should it be duplicated by sending Captain Bernier on a useless expedition to the north?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Captain Bernier goes much farther north than the points I have mentioned. He goes to the Strait of Behring, to Baffin's bay and to much other territory over which we claim jurisdiction, which at present is of very little use perhaps, but tbe value of which we do not know and which may develop.
Who is trying to take it away fx-om you?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Possession is nine points of the law. If we had sent the Mounted roliee twenty years -ago into the Yukon Territory, we would liave to-day more territory than we have. The great

mistake we made was not in attacking sufficient importance to our country. Tke Americans have been muck shrewder in that respect. I do not know whether my hon. friend has seen the last map of the northern country that has been issued at Washington, which shows that the Americans are taking possession of and claiming everything in sight. I do not think they are entitled to it, however.

That does not give them the right to it, because they take possession of it.
Sir WILFRID LAT1RIER. They got Skagway by means of possession. If we had taken possession of it in time they would never have had it.
Is that the way we lost Alaska?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have not lost Alaska, because it belonged to the Russians and was ceded by them to the United States. But there was a disputed territory between tile United States and Canada, and if we had taken earlier the precaution which we have now taken, of sending men into the country to take possession of it, we would have had Skagway to-day. In the last map issued at Washington, I think by the War Department, there are various islands in the north with American names attached to them, conveying the impression that these lands belong to the United States. Captain Bernier goes north in order to put the British flag and assert our authority on this territory, which we claim as ours. If my hon. friend reflects, I think he will agree that it is proper that we should take this precaution. My hon. friend asks who will take away this territory from us. If we had not asserted our sovereignty on Hudson bay four years ago, as we did, white men, attracted by gold or the discovery of the country, would probably have gone in and we would probably have found the Americans disputing 'our jurisdiction on Hudson bay. But by taking the precaution of asserting our jurisdiction we have reached a. point where our authority is no longer disputed. My hon. friend asked why it is now necessary to assert authority since it is recognized and why we should maintain these posts?

I am not finding any fault with the Hudson bay posts. I think we ought to keep them, and according as people flow in the greater is the reason why we should keep them. But I object to this indeterminate charge and this expenditure of Captain Bernier in islands where there is no settlement and never will be any.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
How is my hon. friend sure that there will be no settlement in these northern islands? I understand there are most valuable coal de-282
posits in some of them, and it will be well for us to keep possession of them.
But we are in possession and there is no question of giving them up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, but there is question of somebody else taking possession of them. If we want to assert our jurisdiction in our own country, we must be all the time vigilant. Vigilance is the price, not only of liberty but of security as well. I am making no complaint of our American friends, but they are very enterprising, and if they find anything in any place where there is nobody, they are apt to take possession. For that reason the expenditure connected with the expedition of Cap-taiu Bernier is well warranted. On consideration my hon. friend will come to the conclusion that it is better to spend money in those high latitudes and maintain our jurisdiction.
Whatever is necessary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is necessary. If my hon. friend says we are spending too much that is another question, but we can all agree that it is necessary we should spend something in order to maintain our jurisdiction in these waters, no matter what the cost may be.
With what rifle are the Mounted Police now armed ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Lee-Met-ford and Winchester.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have already explained on former occasions that about seventy-five per cent of the expenditure on the police force is done by contract. Twenty-five per cent is done in the locality where the expenditure is made, but all the large contracts are by tender.

There are a number of posts scattered all over the country in which there are only two and sometimes only one man. They are all subject to some other direction.
