I do not see anything in the Auditor General's Report covering this work. I found one of the buildings at Regina in a very bad state, and the government were replacing the wooden foundations by stone. I found every other building in first-class condition. I think the works were stopped for some reason or other, and I do not see anything about them in the Auditor General's Report.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is all done.
Is it found as easy to recruit new members as formerly and are the new recruits as good a class as the old ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is very difficult to get men and still more difficult to keep them, owing to the prosperity of the country.
Is our force deteriorating ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it is as good to-day as it ever was.

I would like to draw attention to the murder of a policeman at Crows Nest Pass some time ago. The : Mr. FOSTER.
policeman's name was Lewis and he was murdered in the town of Frank. The government have offered a reward of $200 for the capture of the assassin. It seems to me that the government might well offer a reward of $500 or even $1,000. I think some steps should be taken to give a decent reward for the securing of a murderer. It is very important that the police should maintain their standard for enforcing law and order. Along the western border and perhaps in the Crow's Nest Pass there are a number of pretty bad characters, but the police have always maintained law and order in a highly creditable way. When a man is murdered in the discharge of his duties I think the government should not be backward in the granting of reward for the capture of the murderer. A year ago I said in the House that I believed the mounted police were not paid sufficiently in that country. The Prime Minister has stated that it is very hard to keep good men in the service. That must be the case where ordinary labourers are getting $30 to $50 a month with board while the mounted police get only $15 to $25 per month. I believe it would be better if we had a smaller number of men who were better paid, particularly men of long service, because one good man of considerable experience in that country is worth two or three new men not accustomed to the conditions there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A reward of $200 has been offered for the capture of the murderer referred to. We could not have done better as under a standing order the police have power to do that without referring to us but they could not go beyond that amount.	_ t

I think it is only an act of justice to say one word in favour of the mounted police as it is to-day. I am generally pretty hard upon the government and sometimes on my right hon. friend under other circumstances, but I have seen in the west that these men are really a credit to the country. They are well dressed, well kept, well disciplined, and their conduct is splendid. I have had the pleasure of visiting some of the mounted police posts and I found everything in perfect order, in fact their barracks I fancy were equal to anything that you would find in the regular army in England. I consider the force to be very useful. I remember in the old times when my right hon. friend and hi- friends were on this side they criticised the Conservative government for having the mounted police in the Northwest. One Liberal who is now a senator was very severe on that score. I was of the opinion then that we needed the police and I am still of that opinion. I think the maintenance of that force has a salutory effect in that immense country, their presence does much to uphold the peace and tranquility of the west.

As to the question raised by my hon. friend of the pay of the force I have nothing to do with that. I leave that to the generosity of the Prime Minister, but I would point out that the ordinary man who would receive .$40 to $50 a month in that country is not the same kind of man as those who are employed in the police. The mounted police are real soldiers, and many of them quite exceptional men. Their life is a special life and they seem to be perfectly happy. None of those I met made any complaint about pay, and I am sure that many of them would rather work in the foi'ce for $15 or $25 than outside for $40 or $50 a month. I believe they must be well taken care of and well fed and that their lodgings must be kept in perfect condition. On the whole I must congratulate my right hon. friend and his department. Neither in reading the Auditor General's Report nor in travelling in the Northwest do we find a word of graft in that department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have to say to my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Herron) that the question of increasing the pay of the police has been brought to my attention more than once, but on the whole we have not yet seen the advisability of changing the present rate which was established some years ago. There is a great deal, of course, in what was said by the hon. member for Beauliarnois (Mr. Bergeron). The life of the police is a special career, the men are paid from 00 cents to $1 a day, according to a certain scale. They are provided at the end of thirty years with a pension. If a man engages at the age of twenty, then at the age of forty, while still a young man, he can withdraw from the force with a pension and, knowing the country, if he wishes to go into other business he is well equipped to do so. There are a certain number of men who like the life, they are paid a certain amount, they are fed and clothed: they become accustomed to the life and do not care so much for the money because they know they will not be left destitute in their old age. and that they can count on the bounty of the government. On the whole I think they are satisfied. During the twelve years I have been in charge I have not heard a complaint from the force with regard to that. They are too well disciplined of course to send me a complaint even if they thought they had reasonable ground of complaint, but I woul 1 have heard from the comptroller of the force if there had been any grievance in that respect.
Where is the recruiting taking place now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have no special place of recruiting. Recruiting takes place in Ottawa, but the officers are authorized to take men. We have received applications from all parts of the British 282J
empire, but of late years, when we wTere not increasing the force, we have not thought of taking any from outside of Canada as there was no necessity for doing so.

What is the matter with the man who inspects the boots ? I see that under the head of contingencies there is the following item :
Clerical and other assistance, including $50 a year to pay W. Cooch for inspecting letter carriers' boots, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.

This man has been employed in the department for several years. We have to provide the boots for the letter carriers and Mr. Cooch, -who has been em-

ployed as a packer and sorter since 1882 and who is an old shoemaker and well qualified for the work, inspects the boots.
Do I understand that all these boots are brought here ?
We call for tenders in the different cities and if the prices are found to be acceptable we give an order. The boots are brought here and distributed.

If these boots are made in Toronto or Montreal why should they be sent here and sent back again either to Montreal or Toronto ? The expense would be a great deal more than the salary and travelling expenses of a man sent out to inspect them.

They are sent by mail cars and it does not cost the department a cent. It is for the better administration of the department. We have to look after the uniforms in the same way. The uniforms are made in this city but last year they were made in Toronto and sent here. We have nearly 600 or 700 letter carriers and we have to test the boots and clothing. Sometimes we have complaints. This year we had a complaint about our suits and if we did not have the contractors in Ottawa under our own eye probably the complaints would be more numerous, but in consequence of having the clothing made in Ottawa and tested here we avoid a good deal of criticism.
Will the minister make a statement as to the irregularities in the post office service in western Canada?

I saw it stated in the Toronto ' Globe ' and the Toronto ' World ' recently that robberies to the amount of $12,000 had been committed in the Winnipeg post office, but our inspector has reported that this statement is not true. Sometime ago a young man in the Winnipeg post office misappropriated $900, pleaded guilty, and his father refunded the amount and the boy went away. One of the British mail bags disappeared from a station between Montreal and Winnipeg some time ago and we expect to locate the culprit. Fortunately the money orders contained in some of the letters could not be cashed and duplicates are available for those who are properly entitled to them.
What action was taken with regard to the young man in Winnipeg who was convicted and whose father refunded the money ?

I should not have said that the boy pleaded guilty. He was strongly suspected however and the father paid the money that was missing. AVe surround the services with every safeguard, and in comparison with the enormous number of money letters and the great number of employees in the service all over the country
the offences have been comparatively few in recent years. AA7hen a man is found guilty he is sent to the penitentiary. In a recent case in Montreal a man was arrested, brought before the police magistrate, and sentenced to three years in the course of twenty-four hours.
Do I understand that the minister has appointed inspectors to some of the outside districts ?

When the amendment to the Post Office Act is passed I intend to appoint a financial superintendent, not an inspector. The expansion of the postal service especially in the west gives our local inspectors as much work as they can do in other directions and the book-keeping is so complicated that we must have a special man to instruct the different postmasters. It is my intention to appoint Mi*. Johnston, a reliable officer who has been thirty-five years in the service. He is now chief accountant at Ottawa and he will select his clerks specially adapted for the work in the large post offices. They will follow his instructions and so we will have uniformity throughout the Dominion.
Is he a very good accountant ?
Yes, he is quite an authority. He has been asked by one or two other departments to help them.
Why did you not send him to the Marine Department ?
He was probably too busy in our own department.
There are a number of matters I wish to call attention to in connection with the Post Office Department, but as I do not wish to delay the proceedings now I shall avail of another opportunity.
How many male employees are provided for in this item.
And how many ladies.
About 100. The ladies are specially proficient in certain work and young men would not accept the salaries paid for such work.
Did the minister read the Report of the Civil Service Commission on that subject ?
Yes.
The report is that the employment of ladies prevented young men from going through the lower grades and obtaining the higher positions.

Some people criticise the employment of ladies in the departments, but I found the ladies there and as they

are rendering very good service I do not think I should displace them. My individual opinion is that I would rather have university trained young men in the service, but it is very difficult to get young men speaking both languages which is a useful accomplishment in our department which deals with all the provinces in the Dominion. The ladies are employed in typewriting and shorthand writing, and young men who have had a university course will not spend their lives at that occupation. For such duties, I am bound to say, the young ladies in our department give very faithful and efficient service.

I do not want to be understood as opposing the employment of these young ladies. They probably perform their duties as well as young men would perform them and at much lower salaries. But I was very much impressed with the statement in the report of the Civil Service Commission that in the different departments young men are not being trained for the higher positions, as would be the case if they commenced at the bottom of the ladder. That is the point I wanted my hon. friend to ' explain. Could my hon. friend say how long his department has employed young ladies?

I think for about twenty years. We have some young ladies, still young, who entered the department twenty years ago. My hon. friend will remember that ten or fifteen years ago a general movement began on the part of banks and other large financial institutions for the employment of young ladies in large city offices. With regard to the young ladies in the department, I repeat that I have no reason to complain, although of late I have declined to accept the services of any more ladies. I think we have reached the high-water mark; we have about a hundred in the department, and I think that is enough. The reason why we have of late years employed so many ladies in the department is not to the credit of the young men, because it is quite difficult to find young men who are willing to pass the civil service examination, while the young ladies are, as a rule, both more willing and more successful than the young men in these examinations. We need young men in the service, but young men want to be employed without passing the examination. When we cannot find the young men, we take the young ladies.

I am surprised to hear my hon. friend say that he cannot find young men. I was under the impression that there were thousands of young men who had passed the civil service examination waiting for positions.

It is true, some of them have passed the civil service examinations ' Mr. LEMIEUX.
but they do not wish to enter the service unless they get $1,000 at once, whereas the law provides that they must begin with $450 and go up the ladder with an increase of $50 a year. An ordinary labourer comes into the department at $1.25 per day, and can go up to $2.25 per day; but when he passes the civil service examination, he must, according to the law, fall back to $450 a year.
Does my hon. friend say that the young ladies in the different departments are equal to the occasion and in every way as efficient as men?

Perhaps I should have qualified the statement I made. The young ladies in the department fulfil their duties quite creditably in the special class of employment in which they are engaged. It is principally routine work, but they do it well. There are classes of employment in the department which I would not give to ladies, because I do not think, generally speaking, they would be proficient in them.

Would they not be capable of going up to the top of the department?
, Mr. LEMIEUX. My predecessor, Sir William Mulock, established a regulation under which examinations are held every year in the various branches at Ottawa and in the larger city offices, to test the way in which the employees are performing their duties; and on the results of those examinations we promote the officials. As I have stated, the young ladies cannot go above a certain grade.
What is the scale of salaries, and how far can they go?
As a general rule, they commence at $500 and go up to $700 ; but we have two or three ladies in the department who have reached a higher salary.

I imagine that in all the departments in Ottawa there must be about a thousand young ladies employed. I do not understand why the ladies, if they pass the examination, could not climb to the top of the department-why one of these young ladies who have been there for twenty or twenty-five years should not be Deputy Postmaster General. I am considering what ought to be done in the future and am not saying anything about those employed. I am simply talking of the principle in the matter. Who is it that gave the model for the uniforms of the letter-carriers? I do not think anything could be invented that could look worse. If it can be changed without a damage to the constitution of the country, it ought to be.
The present uniform was adopted many years ago. I had first thought that I should be somewhat of a reformer in that direction. I wanted to change the hats, for instance, but I found many objections.
From the contractors?

From the men them' selves. The helmets are used in the British army in southern climates, and our letter-carriers, during certain weeks of' the summer, are in many sections exposed to very high temperature and they find the helmet quite a protection. X wanted to substitute straw hats, but they said to me that, while they were of that opinion in the beginning, they found by expex-ience that the helmet was the best headgear. The uniform is not a bad one. It is not as heavy as it looks. Last year when I visited the Toronto post office and saw the men sorting the letters and going out to deliver them,
I had some of the uniforms weighed and found they were very light. A' good deal of the appearance depends on the men themselves. They ought to keep neat and tidy, and it is my intention later on to give' something more to the men just to teach them to be a little neater and tidier in their wearing apparel. They should have creased trousers and clean shining boots.
Have they only one uniform ?
They have a winter one and a summer one and they have oilcloth coats.
What cities are entitled to letter-carriers?
He is not a manufacturer.
He is a large shoemaker.
He has a retail store and is a shoemaker as well.
Yes, he has a large store on St. Catherine street, and he has besides a large establishment where he employs many men.
If he is the lowest tenderer he is entitled to the contract. I know the man, and if he undertakes a contract he will carry it out.
Each carrier goes to Lecompte and has his measure taken and the boots are made to order.
What is the price.
How many letter carriers in Montreal?
380 in round numbers.
Is there a contract let in each city by tender or is this contract for the whole Dominion?
No, in each large city we give a contract to the lowest tenderer.
How long does it continue?
For a year.

Last year I made new regulations. Cities whose population is 12,000 and whose revenue is $20,000 are entitled to letter carriers. I may tell my hon. friend that some cities which are entitled to letter delivery object to the system because it prevents the men, and especially the ladies, from going out to the post office and stopping at the shops en route.
I would like my hon. friend to inquire from Valleyfield whether they would like to have letter carriers or not. Valleyfield has the population and the revenue as well.
The population, according to the information given me by my hon. friend is there, and I shall inquire as to the revenue.
How are the boots purchased?
By contract after public tender.
Are they purchased wholesale?
They are not purchased indiscriminately. We have a contract and the boots are made to order after measurements are taken.
With what firm?
With Lecompte in Montreal.

I am surprised that the minister, in the face of the Auditor General's Report, would say that all these boots are purchased in Montreal. W hen Sir Wm. Mulock was Postmaster General he resorted to one of the pettiest jobs of patronage and gave to Aurora in his riding the patronage of the whole department. The minister says these boots are purchased by contract in Montreal. Do the facts bear that out? Let me show by the schedule what is purchased in Aurora, simply to give the benefit of the patronage to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) in whose constituency that town is situated.
What volume ?

belts, 100 at 75 cents; sheepskin washers, 3* gross, $4.20, $204.20.
Watson, Win., Aurora: letter carriers' hoots, 46 pairs at $4.50, $207.
Watson, Wm., Aurora, letter carriers' boots, 13 pairs at $4.50, $58.50.
Boots for letter carriers at $4.50 per pair: Charles Tilley & Son, Toronto, 69 pairs, Wm. Watson, Aurora, 80 pairs, $360,
They are repaired in Ottawa and all the large cities. There are three or four different parties in Ottawa repairing mail bags.
It seems odd they Should have to be carted from Toronto or up to North York.
Aurora is a stone's throw from Toronto.

Not by any means. In order to make the patronage as useful as possible, a fair amount of this work is thrown into Newmarket. It is all a question of patronage on the same lines as the giving to the Office Specialty Company at Newmarket, $350,000 worth of business in the last few years. Passing the Supreme Mr. BENNETT
Court building this last week one can see thrown out on the waste heap splendid hardwood and clear pine cases with drawers and bronze handles, with letters on them, thrown out of the departments in order that the Office Specialty Company of Newmarket could make sales to the department.
What are they doing with that?	'

Smashing it up for firewood. Why cannot the minister buy letter-carriers' boots In Toronto or Montreal?
, Mr. LEMIEUX. I do not see what objection there is to distributing here and there throughout the country what my hon. friend calls patronage, which is simply what is needed for the department. I take issue with the hon. gentleman's statements. I am informed that in every case the price paid was the result of tenders asked. Take, for instance, the case of Tilley & Son, Toronto, to whom reference has been made and who sold boots at $4.50 per pair. That is the price paid in Montreal and every one knows it is not an exaggerated price. There is nothing here to show the department has paid an excessive price. Is there any reason why we should concentrate, or to use a new expression, Bovrilize the patronage in one city? If tenders are asked what objection is there to some of the work being done in Aurora or Newmarket.
Who were the competitors for the supplying of these goods for Hamilton, Kingston and Montreal besides Watson of Aurora, and what were the respective rates at which they tendered?
I could not give off-hand the competitors, but I may say that the lowest price was accepted in each case.
Were they advertised in the newspapers ?
Would my hon. friend approve of my hon. friend spending $200 or $300 to advertise for tenders in the case, for instance, of this item of $211 for forty-seven pairs of shoes?
Then it is simply the favoured few, those on the patronage list?
When reliable firms are called upon to tender and when the price is fair as this price is, $4.50-

Does my hon. friend consider Tilley & Son, of Toronto, a large wholesale house? I think their principal business is dealing in shoe findings.
I know the firm, it is a small place. Is it true that the men leave their measures and have the shoes made to order?

Yes, the measures are taken and sent to the makers. I know that is the case in regard to the uniforms which

are made here in Ottawa. The firm making them do not establish a branch in each city where we have a letter-carrier service, but they send their cutter to each city and he takes the measurements of each man ; the uniform is then made to order here where they have their establishment. The same thing applies to the shoes.
And you are paying retail prices for all your shoes and getting no better shoes than you can buy ready made? Forty years ago you could get better shoes made to order.
We do not buy readymade.

I do not care whether you do or not. You can get as good shoes ready-made as to order, if you pay the price. I have been dealing in shoes for forty years. We used to make many shoes to order, we would keep ten to twelve men busy, but now you can get a much nicer shoe ready-made than you can get made to order. I venture to say that not one in ten of the membei's of this House have shoes made to order now.
Are you sure of that ?
That is my experience in my part of the country.
My hon. friend wears American shoes?

I do not wear American shoes. Geo. T. Slater, the Slater Company and McCready & Company are leading houses where you can get as good shoes as in the United States and cheaper than in the United States. You can go to the wholesale manufacturers and get them made at different widths. You can get a narrow width or a middle width, five or six diflerent widths so as to fit any foot. I see that these boots are being bought in the same way as goods have been bought for the Marine and Fisheries Department, that is at retail. No one will say a word against Tilley & Sons, who are a very respectable firm and who no doubt will furnish a first-class shoe. But the chances are that they take the orders and get some wholesale men to furnish them, and you are paying middlemen's profits.

On S-54 there is an item, J. Fleury's Sons, Aurora, newspapers and parcel receptacles, and so forth, $4,719.39. Was there any competition in that line, or are they handed over to the president of the North York Liberal Association ?
No, there is competition.
When the minister comes to his estimates again, will he bring down the names of all those who competed for these articles ?

With regard to the items of S-64, my hon. friend from Lennox and Addington (Mr. Wilson) says that these goods were not made in Victoria where they were distributed. I see that goods of this class are made in many places. For instance H. Leger, Ottawa : letter carriers' boots, 25 pair at $4.50. J. W. Wright, Ottawa, letter carriers' boots, 26 pair at $4.50. It strikes me that it would be better to allow shoemakers who want to get orders the privilege of tendering.
Is the price too high ?

I am not a shoemaker, I do not know. It seems to me that if tenders were sent all over Canada, for instance, to the Mr. McCready firm in Montreal, one of the largest firms in Canada in this line of goods, you might probably get boots for $3 which you are paying here $4.50 ; you could get them cheaper on account of buying a large quantity at the same time. Then the country would save $1.50 each pair on boots. It seems to me that the department should look at the subject from an economical point of view. I see also that uniforms are bought in the same way.
Uniforms for letter carriers: blue melton trousers, 27 pair at $3; blue melton tunics, 16 pair at $5.15; overcoats, 10 at $6.30; pea jackets, 6 at $6.30.
But there is no name given to show who they were purchased from. On page S-62 I find another case of a purchase without any name being given.

They are all purchased from the men who have the contract. The uniforms to which my hon. friend refers as having been bought without any name being given, are all bought from NO el & Chevrier, who have the contract for uniforms for the whole Dominion. It sometimes happens that letter carriers are appointed over and above the number that were specified when the contract was given, and of course these have to be supplied afterwards. But they are supplied at the same price as the other uniforms and the lowest tender was accepted.

At the Ottawa post office I find another item :
Uniforms for letter carriers: * blue melton trousers, 38 pairs at $3; blue melton tunics, 18 at $5.45; overcoats, 9 at $6.30; pea jackets, 9 at $6.30.

I will explain why orders are given sometimes for different numbers. The uniforms are not all delivered at one specified period of the year. For in-

stance, a man comes into the service at the beginning of tbe summer and gets a uniform. If he comes into the service in the middle of the summer he will get his second uniform only at the middle of the summer. We cannot apply the same rule as to the delivery of trousers and shoes to every man, because they do not all enter the service at the same time.
I think it would be better to supply them all under one contract.

There is only one contract, and that contract was awarded to the lowest tenderers, Noel & Chevrier. There were five or six tenderers in all. Now some men will enter the service at the end of a season, they will get their summer uniform. The next year they cannot expect another uniform at the beginning of the summer because they have not used long enough the uniform supplied them in the previous summer. That accounts for the difference in the delivery of uniforms. You will see that at one place 100 uniforms are delivered, at another place 30, at another place 35 and so on. This does not prove that there is more than one contractor, it proves that the uniforms are delivered at different times.

The Post Office Department appears to be not quite so generous in dispensing credit where credit belongs, as it is in dispensing patronage to political friends. I had occasion, during the canvass of the election in 1904, to visit a section of the riding I have the honour to represent, which was not served by a post office, and in which there was a very considerable settlement. I saw at once the necessity of some provision being made for these people, and while I was in the vicinity I drew up a petition which was largely signed. The petition was headed by the Rev. Father Mclnenney, who was parish priest at that particular point. This was Bell's Rapids, in the county of Hastings. I presented that petition to the department here, and urged the necessity of establishing a post office at that point. Nothing was done for some considerable time, and I repeatedly wrote to the department urging upon them again and again the necessity of having these appointments made. Finally I received a letter from the then Postmaster General on the 19th of April, in which he says :
I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter expressing the hope that the department might establish a post office at Bell Rapids. In reply I have to state that some time ago on the application of Mr. Henry Pringle, of Belleville

I ask the Postmaster General to note that.
-Instructions were given to establish a post office at Bell's Rapids and the inspector re-Mr. LEMIEUX
ports that the office went into operation on the 1st instant.
I was of course surprised at being informed by the Postmaster General that the post office had been established upon the recommendation of Mr. Henry Pringle. I can quite understand that the government would not give me any credit for being instrumental in having a post office established in my riding, although such is the fact. Shortly after I received this letter Sir Wm. Mulock went to England and I had not an opportunity of calling his attention to the matter. He was succeeded in the office by Mr. Aylesworth and the following questions and replies were put and answered in the House :

1.	When was the post office known as Bell's Rapids established?
2.	Who is the postmaster?
3.	Upon whose recommendation was such office established, and such postmaster appointed, and when?
4.	Were there any other recommendations or applications for establishment of such post office ? If so, by whom, and when ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Bell's Rapids post office was established on April 1, 1905, with John Hicks as postmaster, on the application of the Rev-Father Mclnerney, of Maynooth, the report of an inspector, and the recommendation of Mr. Henry Pringle, of Belleville.
Here we have the statement repeated that the post office was established on the recommendation of Mr. Henry Pringle. When Mr. Aylesworth gave this answer in the House I immediately telegraphed to a newspaper reporter at Belleville asking him to see Mr. Pringle to ascertain whether the statement made by Mr. Aylesworth, and in the letter of Sir Wm. Mulock, was in accordance with the fact. The reporter saw Sir. Pringle and he telegraphed me on the 3rd of May :
Pringle says he knows of no such office. If he ever had any communication with the government he cannot recall it.
The reporter also made a declaration in connection with the matter in which he says :
I am personally acquainted with Henry Pringle, of the city of Belleville, in the county of Hastings.
On the 3rd day of May, 1905, I had an interview with the said Henry Pringle in Belleville when I asked him if he knew where Bell's Rapids post office was or whether there was such a post office in this county to which he answered: ' I know of no such post office.' I then said: ' Have you ever had any communication with the Post Office Department about such office ?' To which he replied: ' 1 cannot recall any, I don't think I did.'
Without explanation it would seem remarkable that Sir Wm. Mulock should


write me as lie dill and that Mr. Ayles-worth should corroborate his statement giving credit to Mr. Henry Pringle, of Belleville, in view of the fact that Mr. Pringle did not even know there was such a post office in the world. I have stated that I considered that this government was more generous in bestowing patronage upon its political friends than in giving credit to a member of this House who might be entitled to it for acting in the public interest, and my statement is based on the fact that in the election of 1904 I was opposed by a man whose name is well known not only in this House but throughout the country, Mr. Byron O. Lott. Mr. Byron O. Lott, as the defeated Liberal candidate, would be entitled to the patronage of this riding.
Where is he now.

Had Mr. Byron O. Lott been still residing in the west riding of Hastings, the answer of the Postmaster General would have been that the post office was established on the recommendation of Byron O. Lott, but Byron O. Lott then and now is sojourning in the United States to escape criminal prosectution for his connection with the bogus ballot boxes. The government could not, therefore, give the credit to Mr. Lott, and being determined not to give the credit to me they looked somewhere else. One would have thought they would have selected the local Liberal member for that district, but he also has been discredited and so they left the riding of North Hastings where this post office is located and went to West Hastings and there selected the defeated Liberal candidate in the legislature and gave him the credit for establishing this post office at Bells Rapids. I hope the day is past for that manner of establishing post offices and bestowing the credit for establishing them. I do not attribute any of this to the present Postmaster General, but 1 do hope that the course pursued by Sir Wm. Mu-lock and repeated by Mr. Aylesworth will not be adopted by the present Postmaster General in his administration and that he will give credit where credit is due.
Some resolutions reported.

Before the House adjourns I wish to say that according to arrangements made the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Worthington) will bring up the Ross rifle question on going into Supply. Will the House be moved into Committee of Supply?
